before.label: Women’s history
before.date_label: Nineteenth-century and interwar work; renewed expansion from the 1960s
before.description: Studies women as historical actors and examines work, family, politics, and structures of power. Earlier scholarship, activism, teaching, and documentary collecting precede the field’s expansion alongside later feminist movements. Recovery, institutional growth, rediscovery, and methodological disagreement overlap; this is not a field created from nothing in the 1960s or one account of a shared female experience.

Individual entries distinguish contributions and approaches.

before.label: Holocaust historiography
before.description: Investigates the persecution and murder of European Jews through policies, institutions, ideology, perpetrators, victims, and testimony. Intentionalist and functionalist debates intersect with disputes about representation and remembrance. Survivor scholarship and documentation have earlier roots; these concerns coexist rather than replacing one another in a fixed sequence.

Nations, states and nationalist movements are not interchangeable; European typologies require testing beyond their original cases.

nationalismstudies.people: Reviewed six existing selections and added Hroch, Billig and Yuval-Davis. Smith’s relationship to Gellner is a productive disagreement rather than a simple modernist/primordialist binary. Chatterjee remains a theorist in his own right, and Ranger’s colonial-African chapter is separately attributed.
nationalismstudies.works_and_arguments: Filled Smith’s blank with The Ethnic Origins of Nations (1986) and paired catalogue metadata with his primary Warwick statement. Hroch’s 1985 book and 1993 essay, Billig’s 1995 book, Yuval-Davis’s 1997 book and Chatterjee’s 1993 chapter give distinct contextual readings. Earlier inherited book citations receive scoped checks.
nationalismstudies.internal_distinctions: Added eight approaches: print publics, industrial/literate culture, traditions, ethno-symbolism, comparative movements, colonial difference, routine nationhood and gender. Nations, states and movements remain distinct. Hroch’s phases are neither universal stages nor guarantees of national success.
nationalismstudies.incoming_connections: Reviewed Marxist and modernization connections against Anderson’s excerpt and the Warwick exchange. Added the comparative methodological contribution through Hroch, gender contribution through Yuval-Davis, and Chatterjee’s explicit reverse critique of Anderson’s modular model. No history-of-technology arrow is inferred merely from printing.
nationalismstudies.outgoing_connections: Specified the critique of timeless national histories and the Anderson/Chatterjee exchange; preserved memory and global comparisons. Added Billig’s conceptual resource for everyday cultural inquiry, explicitly without claiming a general cultural-history genealogy.
nationalismstudies.evidence_and_interpretation: Primary Smith statement, selected Gellner reply passages, Hroch pp. 3–7 and Chatterjee scan pp. 4–7 provide substantive argument checks. Book descriptions and metadata retain their limits; the proposed Hobsbawm PDF returned HTML. European typologies and colonial tradition scholarship still need bounded case-level comparison and criticism.

holocaust.people: Reviewed seven existing selections and added Ringelblum, Kaplan, Bauer, Tec, Felman and Laub. Collective wartime documentation and Jewish experiences broaden the perpetrator-centered roster. Goldhagen remains a contested participant; Hilberg is a major synthesizer, not the sole founder of Holocaust knowledge.
holocaust.works_and_arguments: Filled Broszat, Mommsen and Goldhagen’s three empty works. Broszat’s 1977 original, 1979 translation and 1985 reprint are distinguished; Mommsen’s 1986 chapter is metadata-only. Kaplan’s 1998 original differs from the linked 1999 edition; the 1996 symposium differs from its 2001 printing.
holocaust.internal_distinctions: Added nine approaches: wartime documentation, administrative destruction, radicalization, perpetrator debate, daily life/gender, rescue/lives, witnessing, representation and memorials. Historical explanation, source criticism and denial are distinguished. The intentionalist/functionalist dispute neither exhausts the field nor replaces survivor documentation.
holocaust.incoming_connections: Reviewed the inherited Frankfurt/Habermas connection and German social-history comparison without converting their bibliography into passage-level verification. Added Kaplan’s women’s-history contribution and a concrete oral-evidence contribution through Kaplan and Browning’s use of Tec. Dedicated witnessing scholarship supplements the broad oral comparison.
holocaust.outgoing_connections: Clarified the evidence/representation contribution: Broszat’s source criticism is an earlier methodological comparison, not a 1977 response to postmodernism or a claimed reception. Social and political comparisons now identify Browning, Kaplan, Broszat and Bauer. Young’s memorial contribution and the plural representation debate retain their scope; primary Friedländer/Habermas follow-up remains required.
holocaust.evidence_and_interpretation: Read selected Broszat primary passages and Goldhagen/Browning 1996 contributions; visually checked Broszat p. 423 and Browning p. 18. Institutional accounts establish Ringelblum’s documentation; publisher descriptions support Kaplan, Bauer and Felman/Laub. Kershaw and Mommsen remain metadata-only. No claim that every occupied territory, Jewish response or persecuted population is covered.
